name: Columba
knownFor: Irish monk who sailed to Britain on pilgrimage for Christ, founded the monastery on Iona, and in Bede's account turned the northern Picts to the faith.
dates: Sailed to Britain in his forty-second year, two years after the battle of Cooldrevny, in Adomnán's words: 563 in Wentworth Huyshe's reckoning, 565 in Bede's. Huyshe gives his years as 521 to 597; Bede says he died at seventy-seven
place: Ireland by birth; Iona, from which he went among the Picts
role: Monk; founder and abbot of Iona

traces: Bede says many monasteries in Britain and Ireland had their beginning through his disciples from Iona and from the house he built in Ireland, the Field of Oaks, and that the Iona house was the chief of them all.
Bede says the abbot of Iona, a priest, ruled the whole province, even its bishops, after the example of Columba, who was a priest and monk and not a bishop.
remembered: Bede calls him a famous priest and abbot, a monk by habit and life, and says he left successors known for their love of God and their keeping of the monastic rule.
Adomnán says his name reached beyond Ireland and Britain to Spain, Gaul, Italy and Rome itself.

At the synod Bede places at Streaneshalch, Whitby, the Irish party called him their most reverend Father Columba; Wilfrid, the priest who spoke for the Roman side, granted he might be a holy man and asked whether he could be preferred to Peter.

uncertain: His life comes from Adomnán, abbot of Iona, whose Life Wentworth Huyshe places between 692 and 697; Huyshe says Adomnán was born twenty-seven years after Columba died. Adomnán says he wrote from older writings and from what faithful old men told him. The Life is a book of prophecies, wonders and visions, and his sayings in it are Adomnán's report.

The year he came to Britain. Adomnán gives his forty-second year, two years after the battle of Cooldrevny; Huyshe dates the battle to 561 and the voyage to 563. Bede gives 565, in the ninth year of Bridius, king of the Picts. The Welsh annals, the Annales Cambriae, put his going to Britain in their year 118, which their editor, John Williams ab Ithel, sets at 562.

His years and age. Huyshe gives 521 to 597. Bede says he died at seventy-seven, about thirty-two years after he came to Britain. The Middle Irish Life in the Book of Lismore gives seventy-seven years and forty-five in Scotland. An Old Irish Life that Huyshe quotes says he was forty-two when he went and thirty-four years in Alba. Whitley Stokes reports that the birthday the Book of Lismore Life gives, a Thursday, 7 December, points to 517 or 523, but Bishop William Reeves thinks 521 most likely. The Annales Cambriae record his birth and death in years their editor sets at 521 and 595.

Why he left Ireland. Huyshe's note says the battle of Cooldrevny was the cause of his exile. His introduction gives the battle as the cause "according to tradition", and calls the tradition that it had something to do with his leaving a constant one. It counts the tales around his exile, the penance among them, as legends. It calls the Old Irish Life's account of a pilgrimage long resolved "perfectly simple and probable". Adomnán names the battle only to date the voyage. He does tell of a synod at Teltown that excommunicated Columba, wrongly as it later proved. William Reeves, as Huyshe reports him, thinks it possibly met in 561, over the battle.

Who gave him Iona. Bede says the Picts gave him the island. Huyshe says the Irish annals name Conall, son of Comgill, king of the Irish of Dalriada in Britain; the Irish annals Huyshe cites are not among the sources used here.

The day of his death. Adomnán puts it in the night after a Saturday, soon after a day in May when he blessed the island. The Book of Lismore Life says the night of Pentecost Sunday. Huyshe gives his feast as 9 June.

Later tradition credits him with poems and hymns. For the Latin hymn Altus Prosator, Huyshe reports the Marquess of Bute's view that the ascription rests on an apparently unbroken tradition and seems open to no serious doubt. The sources used here give only Huyshe's English of some stanzas and poems.

quotationOriginals.work: Adomnán, Life of Saint Columba, Book III, quoting Psalm 33 (34) in the Vulgate, tr. Wentworth Huyshe

quotationOriginals.modern: Here I must stop, at the bottom of this page. Let Baithene write what comes next.
quotationOriginals.printed: "Here", he says, " I must stop at the foot of this page, and what follows let Baithene write."
quotationOriginals.work: Adomnán, Life of Saint Columba, Book III, tr. Wentworth Huyshe
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Adomnán's Latin is not held; rendered from Huyshe's English.

quotationOriginals.printed: the doors open in all haste of their own accord
quotationOriginals.work: Adomnán, Life of Saint Columba, Book II, tr. Wentworth Huyshe
quotationOriginals.uncertain: A wonder, told in Adomnán's voice.

quotationOriginals.modern: My sons, I entrust these last words to you. Love one another without pretense, and live in peace.
quotationOriginals.printed: These my last words I commend to you, O my sons, that ye have mutual and unfeigned charity among yourselves, with peace
quotationOriginals.work: Adomnán, Life of Saint Columba, Book III, tr. Wentworth Huyshe
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Adomnán's Latin is not held; rendered from Huyshe's English. "Charity" is rendered "love", since its modern sense misleads. The sentence goes on with a promise, cut here.

quotationOriginals.modern: But whatever kind of man he was, this much about him we hold as certain. He left successors known for great self-control, for the love of God, and for life under a rule.
quotationOriginals.printed: But whatsoever he was himself, this we know for certain, that he left successors renowned for their continency, their love of God, and observance of monastic rules.

briefReferences: Adomnán, Life of Saint Columba, Book III, tr. Wentworth Huyshe: his last day, the Psalter, "they that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing", and Baithene to write what follows; his last words, heard by Diormit alone; the midnight bell, the altar, and the hand raised to bless.

Adomnán, second preface: born of noble parentage; the voyage in his forty-second year, two years after the battle, "to make a pilgrimage for Christ"; never an hour without prayer, reading, writing or work.
Adomnán, Book III: twelve disciples sailed with him.
Adomnán, Book II: King Brude's gates opening "of their own accord", and the king's lasting honor.
Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.4: Durrow before the voyage; he turned the northern Picts to the faith; Iona the chief of his houses; the abbot over bishops; "whatsoever he was himself".
Bede III.3: Aidan, a monk of Iona, sent to Oswald in 635.
Bede III.25: the synod at Whitby, 664; Colman's defense of "our most reverend Father Columba and his successors"; the king's ruling.
Bede III.4 and V.22: Iona kept its custom until 715 or 716.
Annals of Ulster and Annales Cambriae: 562 for the voyage; Huyshe: about 563, and 597 for the death.
World census, Insular / Irish Monastic Christianity: his setting; a church led by abbots rather than city bishops.
